elements.content:
• What is HTML and why it matters for web development

• Learning objectives: document structure, basic tags, and best practices

• Course roadmap and estimated time

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Ms. Lily Chen, and I’m excited to start our first lesson on HTML. Let’s begin with an overview of what we’ll learn today.
First, what is HTML and why does it matter for web development? HTML is the language that structures every web page—you’ll use it to create headings, paragraphs, images, and links.

Our learning objectives for today are three‑fold: understand the basic document structure, become familiar with common tags like <html>, <head>, <body>, and practice best practices for clean, readable code.
Finally, I’ll share the course roadmap and estimated time for each topic, so you know what to expect and can plan your practice accordingly.
Let’s get started—feel free to ask questions at any time, and we’ll build our HTML skills step by step.

elements.content:

• Root <html> with <head> and <body>

• <title> placed inside <head>

actions.text: Alright, let’s start by looking at the overall structure of an HTML document.
First, every HTML page begins with the doctype declaration `<!DOCTYPE html>`. This tells the browser that the file is an HTML5 document.
Next comes the root `<html>` element, which contains two main sections: `<head>` and `<body>`.
This diagram shows the hierarchy: the `<title>` tag lives inside `<head>`, while all visible content—like headings, paragraphs, and images—goes inside `<body>`.
To recap, a basic HTML page includes the doctype, the `<html>` wrapper, a `<head>` with a `<title>`, and a `<body>` with the page’s content. Any questions before we move on?

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Ms. Lily Chen. Today we're going to learn how to create hyperlinks and embed images in our web pages.
First, let's look at the anchor tag. The basic syntax is link text. The href attribute tells the browser where to go when the link is clicked.
A good practice is to use meaningful link text—people should know what they'll get before they click.
Now, for images we use the tag. It needs a src attribute pointing to the picture file and an alt attribute that describes the image for accessibility.
Remember: choose descriptive alt text so screen readers can convey the meaning, and keep your file paths correct.

actions.topic: Why is meaningful link text and descriptive alt text important?
actions.prompt: Think about how these practices help users and search engines.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create the largest heading on a page?
questions.analysis: <h1> defines the most important heading level. <h2> is a lower level, <header> is a structural element, and <title> belongs in the head section for the page title.

questions.question: Select all attributes that are required or recommended for an HTML image element:
questions.analysis: src provides the image URL and is required. alt gives alternative text and is strongly recommended for accessibility. href is used with tags, not . title is optional.

actions.text: Hello everyone! I'm Ms. Lily Chen. Let's take a quick quiz to see how well you grasp the basics of HTML tags we just covered, like headings and images.

For the first question, remember that the biggest heading uses the <h1> tag. It's the top‑level heading, while <h2> is a step down, <header> is a structural element, and <title> belongs in the document head.

For the second question, an element must have a source (src) so the browser knows what picture to load, and an alt attribute is strongly recommended to describe the image for accessibility. The href attribute belongs to links, and title is optional for tooltips.

actions.topic: Why are the src and alt attributes essential for images, and how does using the correct heading level affect page structure?
actions.prompt: Think about accessibility and the logical flow of a web page.

elements.content:
• List tags: <ol>, <ul>, <li>

• Table structure: <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>

• Form essentials: <form>, <input>, <label>, <textarea>, <button>

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into our topic for today: Lists, Tables, and Forms.
First, we have list tags. Use <ol> for an ordered (numbered) list, <ul> for an unordered (bulleted) list, and <li> for each list item.
Next, let's talk about tables. A table starts with <table>, each row with <tr>, header cells with <th>, and regular cells with <td>.
Finally, we cover forms. A form is created with <form>, and inside you can place <input> fields, <label> elements to describe them, <textarea> for multi‑line text, and <button> to submit.
To recap, we learned the three main tag groups: list tags, table structure tags, and basic form tags. Practice each one, and you'll be building structured HTML in no time!

elements.content:
• Semantic tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves accessibility and SEO

• Use proper indentation, meaningful headings, and alt text

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into Semantic HTML and good practices. This will help us write clearer, more accessible web pages.
First, semantic tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer> give meaning to the structure of our page. They tell browsers and assistive technologies what each part does.
Using these tags improves accessibility for screen readers and also boosts SEO because search engines understand the content hierarchy better.
Finally, good coding style matters: proper indentation, clear heading levels, and descriptive alt text for images make our code easier to read and maintain.
To recap, remember the semantic tags we covered, their benefits for accessibility and SEO, and follow the style guidelines for clean, readable HTML. Great job, everyone!

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is most appropriate for marking up the main navigation links of a website?
questions.analysis: The <nav> element is specifically designed to contain a set of navigation links. <section> groups related content, <aside> is for tangential information, and <header> holds introductory content but not necessarily navigation.

questions.question: Select all HTML5 semantic elements that convey structural information about the page content (choose all that apply).
questions.analysis: <article> defines a self‑contained composition, and <footer> represents the footer of a section or page—both provide semantic meaning. <div> and <span> are generic containers without inherent meaning.

actions.text: Now let's check what we've learned about HTML5 structure and semantics. This short quiz will help you see if you can match each tag to its proper role and choose the most accessible markup for a navigation menu.

Remember, the <nav> element is designed specifically for groups of navigation links. Using <nav> tells browsers and assistive technologies that this block contains the main menu, which improves accessibility.

For structural information, semantic tags like <article>, <footer>, and <section> describe the purpose of the content, while generic <div> and <span> do not convey meaning. Choosing the right tags helps both readers and search engines understand your page.

actions.topic: Why is it important to use semantic elements for navigation and page structure?
actions.prompt: Think about how these tags affect accessibility and SEO.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's wrap up what we've learned today with a quick summary and some next steps.

First, we reviewed the overall document structure and the core HTML tags we use to build a page. Second, I encourage each of you to practice by creating your own personal web page—hands‑on practice is the best way to solidify these concepts. Finally, remember the resources we mentioned: the MDN Web Docs and freeCodeCamp tutorials are excellent places to keep learning.
If you have any questions or need extra practice, feel free to ask Alex or me. Keep experimenting, and you'll see how quickly you can build more complex pages. Great job today, everyone!
